concept.name: Descending triangle
concept.definition: A classical consolidation pattern bounded below by a horizontal support line drawn through two or more comparable lows and above by a descending trend line drawn through successively lower highs. It carries a bearish bias — interpreted as distribution against a fixed demand level — and usually resolves as a continuation of the prior downtrend, though it occasionally forms as a top reversal. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Buyers defend a fixed floor while sellers accept lower and lower prices on each rally; the descending ceiling shows supply pressing down until the floor finally collapses.
concept.mechanics: Require at least two comparable reaction lows for the horizontal line and at least two successively lower reaction highs for the descending line (a new high equal to or above the prior high invalidates the pattern). Volume usually contracts during formation and ideally expands on the downside break; broken support often turns into resistance on a retest. The target subtracts the pattern's widest height from the support break.
concept.formula: Price target = B - (H - L), where B = breakout (horizontal support) price, and H - L = the widest vertical distance of the triangle.
concept.failure_modes: Bulkowski's statistics show breakouts are actually upward about 53% of the time, so the textbook bearish bias is weak in practice; throwbacks and pullbacks are common and can trap breakout traders. A break of the upper trend line busts the pattern upward.
concept.misconceptions: That a descending triangle guarantees a downward resolution — historically the breakout direction is close to a coin flip, and confirmation (a close outside a trendline) matters more than the assumed bias.
concept.example: A stock finds support at $45 three times while its rally highs step down from $54; it then gaps below $45 on expanded volume, projecting a measured decline toward $36.
